lead: A generating function packs a whole sequence into one power series, so it can also unpack a recurrence. Multiply the recurrence by xⁿ, sum over every n where it is valid, and each shifted sum collapses into x·G(x) or x²·G(x). What remains is a plain equation in the unknown G(x). Solve it, split the answer into partial fractions, and read aₙ back off the standard series. This gives closed forms quickly, and it explains why Fibonacci numbers are built from powers of the golden ratio.

blocks.text: The recurrence links aₙ to earlier terms. Multiplying by xⁿ and summing turns the whole sequence into one function. Each shift of the index becomes a multiplication by x plus removal of the early terms.

items: Write the recurrence as aₙ = (rest) for n ≥ k, and list a₀, a₁, …, a_{k−1}.
Set G(x) = Σ_{n≥0} aₙxⁿ, the ordinary generating function.
Multiply both sides by xⁿ and sum over n ≥ k, the index where the recurrence is valid.
Replace each shifted sum by x·G(x), x²·G(x) and so on, subtracting the terms already lost.
Solve the resulting linear equation for G(x). It will be a ratio of two polynomials.
Factor the denominator and split G(x) into partial fractions of the form c/(1 − ax)^m.
Expand each fraction with its standard series and add the coefficients of xⁿ.

blocks.text: The method works because every sum is built from the same G(x). The equation is linear in that single unknown, so ordinary algebra finishes the job.
Learn this table by heart. It is where almost every mark is lost.

Two habits protect you. First, sum from the index where the recurrence is stated, not automatically from n = 0. A recurrence given for n ≥ 1 says nothing about a₋₁, so summing from 0 creates a term that does not exist. Second, the nonhomogeneous part must be summed too: for a constant c, Σ_{n≥1} cxⁿ = cx/(1 − x), a series, not the number c.

If you sum from the wrong index, the two sides pick up different extra terms and G(x) comes out wrong. Testing the final formula at n = 0 and n = 1 against the original recurrence catches the slip in seconds.

sections.h3: Partial fractions and reading off aₙ

blocks.text: A rational G(x) splits into pieces whose coefficients are already known.

blocks.where: a is a fixed real number; the coefficient of xⁿ is aⁿ, and the series converges for |x| < 1/|a|.

blocks.text: When G(x) = P(x)/Q(x) and Q(x) has distinct factors (1 − a₁x)(1 − a₂x)⋯, write G(x) = A₁/(1 − a₁x) + A₂/(1 − a₂x) + ⋯. To find Aᵢ, multiply both sides only by (1 − aᵢx), the factor belonging to Aᵢ. Then put x = 1/aᵢ: every other term still contains (1 − aᵢx) and vanishes. So Aᵢ = [(1 − aᵢx)·G(x)] evaluated at x = 1/aᵢ. That is the cover-up shortcut. Equivalently, cancel (1 − aᵢx) out of Q(x) before substituting. Repeated factors need the powers 1/(1 − ax)^m.
Always test the final formula at n = 0 and n = 1 against the values you were given.
Take F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1 and Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ for n ≥ 2. Sum both sides over n ≥ 2.

The left side is Σ_{n≥2} Fₙxⁿ = G(x) − F₀ − F₁x = G(x) − x. The two right sides are Σ_{n≥2} Fₙ₋₁xⁿ = xG(x) and Σ_{n≥2} Fₙ₋₂xⁿ = x²G(x). Substituting gives G(x) − x = xG(x) + x²G(x), so G(x) = x/(1 − x − x²).

Factor 1 − x − x² = (1 − φx)(1 − ψx), where φ = (1 + √5)/2 ≈ 1.618 and ψ = (1 − √5)/2 ≈ −0.618. These satisfy φ + ψ = 1 and φψ = −1, as the expansion demands. Partial fractions give G(x) = (1/√5)·[1/(1 − φx) − 1/(1 − ψx)].
Reading coefficients: Fₙ = (φⁿ − ψⁿ)/√5, Binet's formula. Since |ψ| < 1, the ψⁿ term dies away, so Fₙ ≈ φⁿ/√5. That is why the numbers grow like powers of the golden ratio.

figure.caption: Pipeline for aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2 with a₀ = 1: summing by xⁿ produces G(x), partial fractions split it into two geometric series, and the coefficients give aₙ = −1 + 2·3ⁿ.

spec.title: GF solution pipeline
spec.aria: The recurrence is multiplied by x to the n and summed, giving G of x, which splits into two fractions and yields a sub n equals minus 1 plus 2 times 3 to the n.

examples.question: Using generating functions, solve aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2 for n ≥ 1 with a₀ = 1. Find G(x), split it into partial fractions, and give a closed form for aₙ. Verify the answer at n = 2.
steps: Let G(x) = Σ_{n≥0} aₙxⁿ. The recurrence holds for n ≥ 1, so sum both sides over n ≥ 1.
Left side: Σ_{n≥1} aₙxⁿ = G(x) − a₀ = G(x) − 1.
First term on the right: Σ_{n≥1} 3aₙ₋₁xⁿ = 3x·Σ_{n≥1} aₙ₋₁xⁿ⁻¹ = 3xG(x).
Partial fractions: (1 + x)/((1 − x)(1 − 3x)) = A/(1 − x) + B/(1 − 3x), so 1 + x = A(1 − 3x) + B(1 − x).
Check at n = 2: the recurrence gives a₁ = 3(1) + 2 = 5 and a₂ = 3(5) + 2 = 17; the formula gives −1 + 2·9 = 17. They agree.
examples.check:
a = [1]
for n in range(1, 7):
    a.append(3 * a[n - 1] + 2)
formula = [-1 + 2 * 3 ** n for n in range(7)]
assert a == formula
for v in formula:
    print(v)

traps: Summing from n = 0 when the recurrence starts at n = 1, which invents an a₋₁ that does not exist.
Writing Σ_{n≥1} aₙxⁿ = G(x); the correct form is G(x) − a₀.
Leaving the nonhomogeneous part as the number 2 instead of the series 2x/(1 − x).
Swapping the numerators of the partial fractions, giving 2 − 3ⁿ instead of −1 + 2·3ⁿ.
Using C(n, m − 1)aⁿ for the coefficient of 1/(1 − ax)^m; the correct binomial is C(n + m − 1, m − 1)aⁿ.

quiz.q: Define the ordinary generating function of a sequence a₀, a₁, a₂, …
quiz.a: G(x) = Σ_{n≥0} aₙxⁿ = a₀ + a₁x + a₂x² + ⋯

quiz.q: Explain why Σ_{n≥1} aₙ₋₁xⁿ equals xG(x).
quiz.a: Put k = n − 1. As n runs over 1, 2, 3, …, k runs over 0, 1, 2, …, and xⁿ = x·xᵏ. The sum becomes x·Σ_{k≥0} aₖxᵏ = xG(x). No term is missing: the shifted index k covers 0, 1, 2, …, the entire sequence, so no term of G(x) is lost, and the factor x stands outside the sum.
The coefficient of xⁿ in 1/(1 − ax)² is (n + 1)aⁿ. With a = 2, aₙ = 3(n + 1)2ⁿ.

quiz.q: Solve aₙ = 2aₙ₋₁ + 1 for n ≥ 1 with a₀ = 0 using generating functions.
quiz.a: Sum over n ≥ 1: G(x) = 2xG(x) + x/(1 − x). So G(x)(1 − 2x) = x/(1 − x) and G(x) = x/((1 − x)(1 − 2x)) = −1/(1 − x) + 1/(1 − 2x). Hence aₙ = 2ⁿ − 1. Check: a₀ = 0, a₁ = 1.

quiz.q: A student solves aₙ = 3aₙ₋₁ + 2, a₀ = 1, reaches G(x) = (1 + x)/((1 − x)(1 − 3x)), and reports aₙ = 2 − 3ⁿ. Identify the error.
quiz.a: The partial fractions are correct only as −1/(1 − x) + 2/(1 − 3x). The student attached −1 to the (1 − 3x) factor and 2 to the (1 − x) factor. Correct answer: aₙ = −1 + 2·3ⁿ, which gives 1 at n = 0 as required.

quiz.q: For Fₙ = Fₙ₋₁ + Fₙ₋₂ with F₀ = 0, F₁ = 1, explain why the numerator of G(x) is x and not 1.
quiz.a: The recurrence holds only for n ≥ 2, so the sum starts at n = 2. The left side is Σ_{n≥2} Fₙxⁿ = G(x) − F₀ − F₁x = G(x) − x. Solving gives G(x) = x/(1 − x − x²); the numerator records that a₀ = 0.

beyond: Not for the exam. Generating functions open into analytic combinatorics, where the singularities of G(x) give the growth rate of aₙ without any exact formula. In algorithm analysis they produce closed forms for divide-and-conquer recurrences and for Catalan-type counting of binary trees. In probability the same object appears as a probability generating function, and derivatives at x = 1 give means and variances. Search next for "ordinary generating function", "coefficient extraction partial fractions" and "Binet formula derivation".
